lead: you know the name of the town he left, the brother he does not speak to, and what he wanted at twenty. he has known you for two decades and has never been asked for anything.
sun: the friendship happens at your place because your place has the room, and it has always had the room. nobody negotiated that. what you can put on a table was decided before either of you had a say in it, and twenty years of thursdays have run on it, so the arrangement everyone calls generosity is the shape of a share you were given and have not had to think about since.
moon: the asking was real. you wanted the whole of him early and inside a month you had it, which is what that appetite is for — it finds out, and then it has found out. so he is a subject you completed in your first season of knowing him, and the twenty years since have been maintenance of an answer you already hold.
pull: nobody has ever been able to do you a favour. not him, not in twenty years — there has never been a gap in you the right size for one.
tension: they call it generous and they mean it, which is how you can tell it is not entirely a compliment. the people at that table worked for less than you have and are gracious about the difference every week. what none of them can arrange is a reversal — one evening where you needed the lift, the loan, the sofa. the friendship is intact, unresented, and it has only ever pointed one way.
cost: somebody can be completely known by you before a year is out, and most people go a lifetime without it happening once. nothing about you is kept back for anyone to earn their way into. so what he knows of you is the part that was already visible, and the closest friendship of your life runs on a share neither of you arranged.

lead: ninety seconds on your feet at your sister's engagement, every word of it true, and the family dates things from that evening now. the room scaled what happened to the size of who was saying it.
sun: nothing you do arrives at its actual size. the same ninety seconds from somebody smaller is an awkward moment people talk over on the way to the car, and from you it becomes the thing the evening was. you did not choose the amplification and could not have declined it, and the reading was set before you were upright.
moon: there is no lower setting to apologise in. the letter you wrote was read aloud. the visit was discussed. each attempt to bring the thing back down to its real dimensions has gone out at your dimensions instead, so the repair is now three public events long, and the ninety seconds that started it is the smallest item on the list.
pull: the apology was bigger than the offence, and so was the apology after that. nothing you have ever done has been received at the size it actually was.
tension: the account that stuck is that you could afford it. you had somewhere else to be that night and everyone in the room knew it — the job that was not at risk, the share that arrived without anybody's permission. so the scene gets explained by what you were handed rather than by anything you felt, and the feeling was the only part of the evening that was not decided for you.
cost: people who needed a thing said out loud got it said, at the volume it deserved, by somebody with no stake in being invited back. permanence attaches at your size, though. two years on, people who were not in the building can describe what you did, and the reason for it has not travelled with it.

lead: nine years gone and one lunch back, and by the end of it the room had rearranged itself around you again. nobody voted. your aunt moved down a chair without noticing she had done it.
sun: a quiet way back in was never on offer. a return at your width is an occasion the moment it happens, and nine years of somebody else running things got folded back underneath you inside an afternoon — not because you asked, and not because anyone decided. the seat was still the right shape, and what changed hands changed hands in the ordinary noise of lunch.
moon: you never filed the leaving as an ending, so nothing got arranged for it — no handover, no letter, no last evening. inside, the nine years were a pause, and a pause does not require a goodbye from anyone. so you came back expecting it all to still be there, and the expectation was correct, which is the part that reads to everyone else as confidence.
pull: your cousin held it together for nine years. you were back for one lunch, and by the washing up she was explaining the arrangements to you for approval.
tension: nothing was seized. you did not ask for the chair, or for the calls that now come to you first, and everyone saying how good it is to have you back means it. the trouble is what the nine years have become: your cousin held the whole of it together, and she is already the one describing that stretch as the time while you were away.
cost: leaving for a decade did not cost you the room, and there are people who left for six months and came home to a closed door. the same fact removes the option of a small return: you cannot come back as one more person at the table, so every homecoming of yours has quietly demoted whoever was holding it while you were gone.

lead: the house came to you and nobody said a word about it. four years on, his people are still in it most weekends, and grief and the question of the share are now the same visit.
sun: you were the largest thing at the funeral without doing anything, which is how the traffic got routed. his widow, his brother, the two men he worked with for thirty years — all of them arrived at your door with it, because a place that reads as having room is the place grief goes. no one asked whether there was room. the reading did the asking.
moon: nothing about it comes with a total attached. year four takes what week two took, and the visits do not record themselves as visits — people who leave steadied are not counting, and neither, at any point in this, were you. so his absence gets fed and kept warm in your rooms most weeks, by a crowd that is genuinely lighter on the way out.
pull: his people have somewhere to put it and the somewhere is your house. you have not had one hour of missing him that was not also somebody else's evening.
tension: everybody knows the size of what came to you, so nobody arrives empty-handed. his brother is generous about the will most weekends, out loud, and the generosity is the part you can hear. asking anyone to come less often would close the only place he still gets talked about in the present tense, so nothing gets asked, and four years in you have not been alone in the room he died in.
cost: a man four years dead is still a weekly presence for fifteen people, and that is your doing, though nobody had to organise anything to get it. the house has one setting and it has always been open. so the mourning that was yours has been conducted in company since the day of the burial, and what it is like on your own is still ahead of you.
